title: Texas Twinkies
pitTemp: 225–250°F, then a hot grate to crisp
finish: Bacon crisp, pepper collapsed, glaze set
summary: Jumbo jalapeños stuffed with leftover brisket and cream cheese, wrapped in thick bacon, smoked, then glazed. Hutchins BBQ's leftover-brisket accident.
story: Hutchins BBQ in McKinney started stuffing leftover fatty brisket and cream cheese into the biggest jalapeños they could find, wrapping them in thick bacon, and sending them back through the smoker. A Texas Twinkie is not a halved popper with a smear of cheese. It is a whole pepper, close to a quarter pound of brisket in each one, smoked until the pepper slumps and the bacon renders, then glazed and kissed on a hot grate. Two of them is lunch. Use leftover packer — the point is better than the flat.

items: 8 jumbo jalapeños, 4–5 inches — the biggest you can find
Ice water, optional pinch of sugar in the bath
1 lb leftover smoked brisket, preferably point, chopped small
Kosher salt and coarse black pepper
½ cup sweet Texas-style barbecue sauce

steps.title: T-cut and seed
steps.body: Gloves on. Cut a T into each pepper: a slit down one long side and a short cut under the stem, without cutting through. Open it like a book. Scrape out seeds and white pith. Keep the stem. Soak in ice water 15–20 minutes if you want them milder — a pinch of sugar in the bath helps. Drain and pat dry.

steps.title: Stuff 50/50, don't stir it into mush
steps.body: Cream cheese in the bottom third of each pepper. Pack chopped brisket on top until the pepper is full and just barely closes. About 2 ounces of each per jumbo pepper. Do not mash brisket and cheese into one paste — you want a bite of bark and a bite of cheese.

steps.title: Two slices of thick bacon
steps.body: Thin bacon tears and shrinks off. Wrap each pepper with two thick slices so the seam is covered. Toothpick the ends. Dust with salt and coarse pepper like a little brisket.

steps.title: Smoke low
steps.body: 225–250°F, post oak. Directly on the grate, 2–2½ hours. Flip once if one side is pale. The pepper should be soft and the bacon rendered but not yet shatter-crisp. Internal around 145°F is fine — everything in there is already cooked except the bacon.

steps.title: Glaze and crisp
steps.body: Brush a thin coat of sweet sauce. Move to a hotter grate or skillet, 350°F-ish, 2–4 minutes until the bacon tightens and the glaze tackifies. Rest 5–10 minutes. Pull the toothpicks. Serve hot.

proTips.text: The pepper has to be huge. Grocery jalapeños the size of a thumb make sad little poppers. Mexican markets and the ugly bin are where the rib-sized ones live.
Point meat, not leftover flat. Dry flat plus cream cheese is a brick. Fat is the point of the Twinkie.
Sauce at the end. If you mop it on at 225°F for two hours you steam the bacon and burn the sugar. Smoke first, glaze last, then heat.

milestones.label: Stuffed and wrapped
milestones.hint: Cream cheese down, brisket packed, two slices thick bacon.

milestones.label: Smoked
milestones.hint: 2–2½ hours at 225–250°F. Pepper soft, bacon rendered.

milestones.label: Glazed and crisp
milestones.hint: Sauce, then a hot grate. Rest 5 minutes. Pull the picks.

title: Cast Iron Green Beans with Ham Hock & Potatoes
wood: None — Dutch oven on the stove or over coals
finish: Beans silky, potatoes poke-tender, vinegar in the end
summary: Ham hock pot liquor, whole potatoes, snapped beans. Vinegar last. Taste before you salt.
story: This is pot liquor cooking, not a crisp skillet sauté. The hock simmers first so the broth tastes like smoke and bone before the beans ever hit the pot. Fresh beans go in raw and come out silky. Canned beans wait until the last 20–30 minutes or they fall apart. Country ham is saltier than a hock — cut the bouillon and don't salt until you've tasted.

items: 2 lbs fresh green beans, ends snapped (or 4 cans, drained — see notes)
1 large smoked ham hock, 1–1.5 lbs (or a ½–¾ lb chunk of country ham)
1½ lbs small whole potatoes, scrubbed, skins on
4 cups chicken broth (or 4 cups water + 4 tsp chicken bouillon)
1 Tbsp apple cider vinegar, stirred in at the end

steps.title: Build the pot liquor
steps.body: Ham hock (or country ham) and broth in the Dutch oven, lid on. Gentle simmer 45–60 minutes.

steps.title: Load the pot
steps.body: Lift the meat out. Add onions, potatoes, and fresh green beans. Nestle the meat back on top. Broth should nearly cover; splash in water if short.

steps.title: Simmer low
steps.body: Lid on, low simmer 45 minutes to an hour, until beans are silky and potatoes poke tender.

steps.title: Chop the meat back in
steps.body: Fish out the meat, chop it, stir it back in.

steps.title: Vinegar, then taste
steps.body: Stir in the vinegar, then taste before salting.

proTips.text: It's saltier than a hock — cut the bouillon in half (or use low-sodium broth) and don't add any salt until you've tasted at the end.
They're already cooked. Don't put them in with the potatoes or they'll fall apart. Add the drained cans for just the last 20–30 minutes so they soak up flavor without going mushy.

milestones.label: Vinegar in
milestones.hint: Meat chopped back in. Taste before salt.

title: Pit-Smoked Zesty Mac & Cheese
wood: Hickory, oak, or pecan — not mesquite
summary: Three-cheese sauce, jalapeño heat, panko crust. Smoke it just long enough to kiss it, not bury it.
story: Cheese takes smoke fast. This one lives in a 9x13 or a cast-iron skillet on the pit at 250–275°F with mild wood. Shred your own cheese or the sauce goes grainy. Season a notch louder than you want — the smoke will calm it down.

items: 1 lb elbow macaroni or cavatappi, cooked 2 minutes shy of package time, drained
1 tsp hot sauce, plus more to taste
2–3 jalapeños, diced (leave some seeds for more fire)
Salt and black pepper to taste
1 tsp BBQ rub (or paprika + pinch of cayenne)
½ lb bacon, cooked crisp and crumbled, folded in

steps.title: Fire and pasta
steps.body: Pit at 250–275°F. Mild wood — hickory, oak, or pecan. Not mesquite. Cook pasta 2 minutes shy of done. Drain.

steps.title: Roux, then dairy
steps.body: Melt butter, whisk in flour, cook 1 minute. Whisk in evaporated milk and cream. Simmer until it coats a spoon.

steps.title: Cheese off the heat
steps.body: Melt in cream cheese, then shredded cheeses a handful at a time. Stir in mustard, onion and garlic powder, hot sauce, and jalapeños. Season bolder than you want — smoke mellows it.

steps.title: Pan and crust
steps.body: Fold in pasta. Spread in a greased 9x13 foil pan or cast iron. Toss panko with melted butter and rub; scatter over the top.

steps.title: Smoke, then rest
steps.body: Uncovered on the pit 45–60 minutes until bubbly and golden. Rest 10 minutes so it sets. If it looks dry coming off, stir in a splash of warm cream.

proTips.text: Shred your own cheese. Bagged shreds have starch that turns the sauce grainy.
Don't oversmoke it. Cheese picks up smoke fast — an hour is plenty.

milestones.label: Sauce coats a spoon
milestones.hint: Then pull off heat and melt cheese.

title: Smoked Christmas Ham
summary: Fully cooked bone-in ham, pineapple rings, cherries, and a brown-sugar pineapple glaze. Mild fruit wood. Don't blast it.
story: The ham already took a smoke once at the plant. What you are doing is warming it through and laying on a sticky glaze so the table looks like Christmas. Pin pineapple rings with a cherry in the middle, hold 250°F, and stop at 140°F. Hotter and the sugar scorches; past 145°F and it dries out. The drippings in the foil pan are liquid gold — spoon them over the slices.

items: 1 (8–10 lb) fully cooked bone-in ham (spiral-sliced or shank portion)
1 can pineapple rings in juice (reserve the juice)
¼ cup pineapple juice (from the can)
2 Tbsp Dijon mustard (or yellow for milder)

steps.title: Pit at 250°F
steps.body: Apple or cherry wood — mild fruit smoke suits ham best. It's already smoked once, so don't blast it. Hold 250°F; hotter and the sugar glaze can scorch.

steps.title: Score if you need to
steps.body: If the ham is not spiral-sliced, score the fat in a diamond pattern so the glaze sinks in.

steps.title: Pineapple and cherries
steps.body: Pin pineapple rings all over the ham with toothpicks, a cherry in the center of each ring.

steps.title: First glaze
steps.body: Set the ham in a foil pan (catches the drippings for basting) and brush on a first coat of glaze.

steps.title: Smoke and mop
steps.body: Smoke 2.5–3.5 hours, brushing with glaze every 30–45 minutes, until the inside reads 140°F.

steps.title: Final coat
steps.body: Last 30 minutes: lay on a final thick coat of glaze and let it tack up.

steps.title: Rest and carve
steps.body: Rest 15 minutes tented with foil before carving. Spoon the pan drippings over the slices.

proTips.text: Don't push past 140–145°F internal or it dries out. This is a warm-through, not a cook.
Hold 250°F. The sugar will scorch if you chase heat.
325°F, about 15 minutes per pound, same glaze schedule.

milestones.label: On the pit
milestones.hint: 250°F, apple or cherry, ham in a foil pan.

milestones.label: 140°F
milestones.hint: Final thick coat, let it tack. Rest 15 minutes.

title: Honey-Glazed Smoked Turkey Breast
summary: HoneyBaked-style bone-in turkey breast. Overnight brine, maple smoke at 275–300°F, honey-brown sugar glaze until it crackles.
story: This is the HoneyBaked copy without the spiral slicer. Brine overnight so the breast stays wet through a 275–300°F smoke. Maple is mild and a little sweet — made for poultry. Glaze starts around 145–150°F and gets a fresh coat every 15 minutes. Pull at 160°F. Carryover finishes it at a safe 165°F. Stir extra sugar into the last coat if you want that candy-shell crackle.

items: 2 Tbsp olive oil or melted butter
1 tsp kosher salt if brined (1 Tbsp if not)

steps.title: Brine overnight
steps.body: Stir salt and brown sugar into a gallon of cold water until dissolved. Submerge the breast and refrigerate 8–12 hours. No fridge room? Inject melted butter whisked with chicken broth throughout the meat instead.

steps.title: Dry and season
steps.body: Rinse the brine off and pat the breast VERY dry. Rub with oil, then season all over. Optional: work some seasoned butter under the skin.

steps.title: Smoke on maple
steps.body: Pit at 275–300°F with maple wood splits. Mild and slightly sweet, made for poultry. Don't smoke poultry below 275°F — it needs to move through the danger zone.

steps.title: Start the glaze
steps.body: Smoke until the thickest part hits 145–150°F (about 2–2.5 hours). Brush on the honey glaze, then re-glaze every 15 minutes.

steps.title: Pull and rest
steps.body: Pull at 160°F internal — carryover takes it to a safe 165°F. Rest 20–30 minutes tented with foil before slicing. For extra HoneyBaked-style crackle, stir 2 Tbsp sugar into the final glaze coat.

proTips.text: Don't smoke poultry below 275°F. Low-and-slow is for pork and brisket, not turkey.
Stir 2 Tbsp extra sugar into the last glaze coat and let it tack. That's the candy shell.
Skip the bucket. Inject a stick of melted butter whisked with ½ cup broth.

title: Ember Finishing Glaze
servings: ~1¼ cups — racks or a pulled butt
pitTemp: Warm only — do not reduce it into candy
finish: Thin, pourable, sets tacky — meat still shows through
summary: Sweet-tangy finishing glaze for ribs or pork butt. Thin coat. The pork has to shine, not the bottle.
story: A glaze is a last coat, not a sauce bath. Vinegar and mustard cut the molasses so it doesn’t read candy. Honey gives shine. Worcestershire keeps it savory. Warm it until it loosens — it should coat a spoon and still run. On ribs, one thin pass in the last 15–20 minutes so it sets tacky. On a pork butt, toss the pull while the meat is hot and stop when you can still see bark. Extra in a bowl. If you can’t taste smoke through it, you used too much.

steps.title: Warm until it runs
steps.body: Stir over low heat just until the sugar dissolves and the glaze loosens. Do not boil it down. If it sits in a sheet, thin with vinegar or juice.

steps.title: Ribs — late and thin
steps.body: Last 15–20 minutes on the pit. One thin coat. Lid shut so it sets tacky, not wet. A second kiss only if the first soaked in.

steps.title: Pork butt — after the pull
steps.body: Toss the hot pulled pork with a light coat. Bark should still show. Pass the rest in a bowl.

proTips.text: Sauce is a finishing coat. If you need a soup of it to make the ribs taste like something, the rub and fire didn’t do their job.
Sugar late. Early glaze scorches. Late glaze shines.
If you can’t taste the smoke through it, wipe some off and serve the rest on the side.

milestones.label: Warmed thin
milestones.hint: Coats a spoon and still runs.

milestones.label: Thin coat
milestones.hint: Ribs last 15–20 min, or tossed on hot pulled pork.

title: Apple-Peach Pork Injection
servings: ~3½ cups — enough for an 8–10 lb butt
pitTemp: Warm the liquid only — do not boil
finish: Sugar and salt dissolved, cooled, strained
summary: Apple juice plus peach nectar for pork butt. Enough tang that the fruit doesn’t read candy-sweet.
story: Apple juice is the classic pork-injection base. Peach nectar on top of it makes the mix read Southern instead of just sweet. The vinegar does quiet work — just enough bite to keep all that fruit and sugar from going candy. Warm it so the salt and brown sugar disappear, cool it, strain it, then grid the butt. Rest in the fridge a couple hours or overnight, then rub and smoke as usual. Pork butt is forgiving. Don’t overthink the pattern.

steps.title: Warm and dissolve
steps.body: Warm the mix gently and stir until the sugar and salt disappear. Do not boil — you want it dissolved, not cooked down.

steps.title: Cool and strain
steps.body: Cool to room temp. Strain so powder clumps and any pulp don’t clog the needle.

steps.title: Grid the butt
steps.body: Inject in a 1-inch grid all over. Pork butt is forgiving — don’t overthink the pattern. Some leakage is normal; wipe it and keep going.

steps.title: Rest, then rub
steps.body: Fridge a couple hours or overnight. Then rub and smoke as usual.

proTips.text: The vinegar is doing quiet work here — just enough tang to keep all that fruit and sugar from going candy-sweet.
Peach reads more Southern than straight apple juice ever will. Kern's or any canned nectar is fine.
Strain. A clogged injector mid-butt is how you make a mess and skip half the meat.

milestones.label: Dissolved
milestones.hint: Warm, stir, sugar and salt gone.

milestones.label: Cooled and strained
milestones.hint: Room temp. Fine mesh so the needle stays clear.

milestones.label: Injected
milestones.hint: 1-inch grid. Rest in the fridge, then rub.

title: Ember Brisket Injection
servings: ~2 cups — one packer, heavy on the flat
pitTemp: Warm the liquid only — do not boil
summary: Reduced beef, a shot of coffee, and quiet umami. For a packer — especially the lean flat. Not a phosphate crutch.
story: This is brisket injection. The flat is where it earns its keep. Reduced bone broth, a little coffee, Worcestershire, and a drop of fish sauce. You will not taste coffee or fish. You will taste deeper beef. Season the inside of the lean. Go light on the point — that side already has fat. A clean fire and a real rest still have to do the work. Then salt, pepper, and the same post-oak cook you were going to run anyway.

items: 1½ cups unsalted beef bone broth, reduced by about a third (or 1½ cups water + 1½ Tbsp roasted beef base)
¼ cup strong black coffee, cooled
1 tsp fish sauce (Red Boat or similar — you will not taste fish)
½ tsp kosher salt (skip or cut if the base is already salty)
1 Tbsp melted beef tallow, optional — strain well

steps.title: Warm and dissolve
steps.body: Warm just enough to dissolve the powders and melt the tallow if you are using it. Do not boil.

steps.title: Cool and strain
steps.body: Cool to room temp. Fine-mesh strain. Tallow and coffee fines clog needles. Mix fresh — don’t park overnight with the fat in it.

steps.title: Inject the flat
steps.body: 1-inch grid through the brisket flat. Lighter pass on the point. Leakage is normal. Wipe and keep going.

steps.title: Rest, then rub
steps.body: Fridge 2–12 hours. Then salt and pepper and the same fire you already trust.

proTips.text: This is flavor for the flat, not a crutch. If the fire is dirty and the rest is short, no syringe saves lean brisket.
Coffee is roast. Fish sauce is quiet MSG. Neither should announce itself. If you can name them in the slice, you used too much.
Strain twice if you use tallow. A clogged injector is how you season three spots and skip the rest of the flat.

Don't save this one for brisket. Venison is the leanest meat you'll put on the pit — a backstrap or a hindquarter roast will dry out on you fast. Hit it with this injection first and it stays juicy all the way through the cook.

milestones.label: Flat injected
milestones.hint: 1-inch grid on the lean. Light on the point. Rest, then rub.

title: Holiday Smoked Ham
finish: 135–140°F internal — already cooked, don’t roast it dry
summary: City ham on the pit with a clove-cinnamon glaze. Warm it, smoke it, glaze late. Not a 12-hour hostage.
story: A grocery city ham is already cured and cooked. The job is gentle smoke and a holiday glaze, not another all-day cook. Score the fat, stud a few cloves, run apple or pecan at 250–275°F until the center is 135–140°F. Then the glaze: brown sugar, cider, Dijon, honey, cinnamon, and just enough clove. Two thin coats in the last 20–30 minutes. Rest 20 minutes. Clove and cinnamon should be a hello, not a Yankee Candle.

items: 1 city ham, 10–12 lb, spiral or bone-in
8–12 whole cloves for studding — not a full coat
⅓ cup apple cider or pineapple juice
¼ tsp ground cloves (or 4 whole cloves, fished out after warming)

steps.title: Score and stud
steps.body: Pat the ham dry. Score the fat in diamonds — into the fat, not the meat. Stud a few cloves in the diamonds. A handful. Not the whole ham.

steps.title: Warm with clean smoke
steps.body: 250–275°F, apple or pecan, cut-side down. A 10–12 lb ham is often 2½–3½ hours. Start probing at 2 hours. Target 135–140°F. It is already cooked.

steps.title: Warm the glaze
steps.body: Stir the glaze over low heat until the sugar dissolves. Thin enough to brush. Fish out whole cloves if you used them.

steps.title: Two thin coats
steps.body: Last 20–30 minutes. Brush one coat. Let it set. Brush a second. Pull at 140°F. Rest 20 minutes before slicing.

proTips.text: Past 145°F a city ham starts giving the water back. Warm it. Don’t cook it twice.
If it smells like potpourri you used too much clove. A quarter teaspoon ground is plenty for a cup of glaze.
Cold slices, biscuits, or fried ham with eggs. Don’t microwave a spiral — it weeps.

title: Pitt Style Amber Ham
finish: 145–155°F after the amber sauce — thin, not candy
summary: Pittsburgh ham barbecue with smoke first. Thin sweet-tangy red sauce that cooks down amber. Chipped onto a toasted kaiser.
story: In the Burgh this is not pulled pork. It is chipped ham in a ketchup-vinegar-brown-sugar sauce piled on a kaiser. Ember smokes a bone-in ham first so you get bark, then finishes it in that same thin red sauce until it turns amber and sticky. Same sandwich. Better fire. The sauce stays thin — it soaks the meat; it is not Kansas City paste.

items: 1 bone-in smoked ham, 7–10 lb (or 1½–3 lb chipped chopped ham for the fast version)
Yellow mustard or oil as binder
Ember House Rub, or brown sugar, paprika, black pepper, garlic, pinch of cinnamon
½ small onion, minced (or 1 tsp onion powder)
Optional: ½ cup amber ale, splash of pickle juice, pinch of cayenne
Kaiser rolls or soft hamburger buns, toasted

steps.title: Rub the ham
steps.body: Pat dry. Light binder, then rub.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: 250°F over apple or cherry until about 130–140°F internal. Spritz with apple juice if the surface dries.

steps.title: Make the amber sauce
steps.body: Melt butter, sweat the onion, add ketchup, water, vinegar, brown sugar, Worcestershire, mustard. Simmer 10 minutes until it thins and turns amber-red. Ale at the end if you use it.

steps.title: Finish in the sauce
steps.body: Move the ham to a pan. Pour sauce over and around. Cover loosely. Continue at 250–275°F until 145–155°F and the glaze is lacquered.

steps.title: Chip and pile
steps.body: Rest 20–30 minutes. Slice thin or chip it. Toss in the pan sauce. Pile on toasted rolls. Relish on top. Fast version: skip the smoke, simmer sauce 10 minutes, stir in chipped ham, heat 5–7 minutes.

proTips.text: The sauce should stay thin. If it sits like molasses you cooked it too long.
Thick-sliced ham is the wrong texture. Chip it until it looks like confetti.
No smoker? The skillet version is the original lunch-counter sandwich. Don’t skip the toasted roll.

milestones.label: Amber sauce
milestones.hint: Thin, red going amber. Ten-minute simmer.

milestones.label: Glazed and chipped
milestones.hint: 145–155°F. Thin slices. Relish on the roll.

title: Bacon-Wrapped Venison Tenderloin Bites
summary: The first thing gone at every deer camp. Tenderloin medallions wrapped in bacon, kissed with smoke, finished with Ember Finishing Glaze.
story: These don't make it to the table half the time. Thin bacon, a sweet-heat rub, and a hot enough pit to render the fat before the venison sees 140. That's the whole trick — everything else is just getting out of the way.

items: 1 1/2 to 2 lb venison tenderloin, silverskin removed
12 slices thin-cut bacon, cut in half

steps.title: Cut medallions
steps.body: Cut the tenderloin into 1 1/2-inch medallions, all roughly the same thickness so they cook even.

steps.title: Season
steps.body: Mix the rub and coat every medallion on all sides.

steps.title: Wrap
steps.body: Wrap each medallion with a half-slice of bacon and pin with a soaked toothpick. Snug, not strangled.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: 275°F for 45 to 60 minutes, until the bacon renders and starts to crisp and the venison reads 130-135°F inside.

steps.title: Glaze
steps.body: Brush on the Ember Finishing Glaze during the last 10 minutes so it tacks up instead of burning.

steps.title: Rest
steps.body: Rest 10 minutes, pull the toothpicks, and serve warm.

proTips.text: Thin bacon beats thick here. Thick bacon won't render before the tenderloin overcooks.
Past 140°F these dry out fast. Pull at 130 and let carryover do the rest.
Make a double batch. You'll thank yourself.

title: Smoked Venison Jerky
summary: Real smoked jerky — chewy, peppery, with actual smoke on it. The cure keeps it safe, the low smoke keeps it tender.
story: Store jerky is a rumor of meat. This is the real thing — venison sliced thin, cured right, and smoked low until it bends and cracks. A splash of pineapple juice in the marinade adds a sweet-tangy note, but mind the clock: those enzymes work fast. Takes a day of waiting and an afternoon of watching, and you'll never buy a bag again.

items: 3 lb venison roast (eye of round or hindquarter), all fat and silverskin trimmed
1/2 tsp Prague Powder #1 (pink curing salt) — do not skip
1 tsp red pepper flakes (optional, for heat)

steps.title: Slice
steps.body: Partially freeze the roast 1 to 2 hours until firm. Slice 1/4-inch thick against the grain.

steps.title: Marinate
steps.body: Whisk everything else into the marinade and coat the slices completely in a zip bag or covered pan.

steps.title: Wait
steps.body: Refrigerate 8 to 12 hours, turning once. The pineapple's enzymes work fast — don't push past 12 hours or the meat goes mushy.

steps.title: Rack up
steps.body: Lay the slices on oiled smoker grates with space between them. Pat lightly — tacky, not dripping.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: 170-180°F for 4 to 6 hours. Start checking at 4: it's done when a cooled piece bends and cracks but doesn't break, and reads 160°F inside.

steps.title: Store
steps.body: Cool completely, then bag it. Refrigerate for long keeping — it'll last weeks in the fridge, if it survives the week.

proTips.text: The cure is food safety, not optional. It keeps the low-temp smoke safe.
Uniform slices = uniform jerky. The freezer trick is the whole secret.
Judge doneness on a cooled piece — hot jerky always feels softer than it is.

milestones.label: Done
milestones.hint: Bends and cracks. Cool, bag, refrigerate.

title: Smoked Venison Backstrap with Coffee-Chile Rub
summary: The best cut on the deer, treated like it matters. A dark coffee-chile crust, gentle smoke, then a screaming-hot sear. Slice it pink and watch people go quiet.
story: Backstrap is the cut you don't waste on a crowd-pleaser — it's the one you cook when you want people to remember the meal. Coffee and chile make a crust dark as bark, the smoke stays in the background, and the reverse sear keeps it pink edge to edge.

items: 1 whole venison backstrap, 2 to 3 lb, silverskin fully removed
2 Tbsp olive oil or yellow mustard (binder)
Compound butter (butter mashed with garlic and thyme), optional

steps.title: Trim
steps.body: Remove every bit of silverskin — it won't render and chews like rubber. Pat dry.

steps.title: Rub
steps.body: Coat with the oil or mustard, then the mixed rub, generously. Rest at room temp 30 to 45 minutes while the pit heats.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: 225°F until the internal temp hits 115-120°F, about 45 minutes to an hour.

steps.title: Sear
steps.body: Screaming hot — cast iron, grill grates, or right over the coals — 60 to 90 seconds per side, until the crust darkens and the center reads 130-135°F.

steps.title: Rest
steps.body: Rest 10 to 15 minutes tented in foil.

steps.title: Slice
steps.body: Slice against the grain, 1/2-inch thick. Top with compound butter if you're feeling fancy. Serve immediately.

proTips.text: Silverskin is the enemy. Take your time trimming — it's the difference between great and chewy.
Venison is lean — give the backstrap a pass with the Ember injection before the binder and rub. It stays juicy all the way through the sear.
The reverse sear is what keeps it pink edge to edge instead of gray-banded.
Trust the thermometer, not the clock.

title: Smoked Leg of Lamb with Garlic, Rosemary, and Pesto
summary: Lamb on the smoker is a sleeper hit. Garlic and rosemary pressed into a scored fat cap, gentle smoke, pulled pink, finished with fresh pesto.
story: The people who say they don't like lamb just never had it like this. Score the fat cap, work the garlic-rosemary paste in deep, let the smoke do the rest — then spoon fresh pesto over the slices so it stays bright.

items: 1 bone-in leg of lamb, 5 to 7 lb
3 Tbsp fresh rosemary, chopped (or 1 Tbsp dried)
1 cup basil pesto, for spooning over the slices

steps.title: Trim and score
steps.body: Trim the leg of surface silver and excess fat, leaving a 1/4-inch fat cap. Score the cap in a diamond pattern so the rub gets in.

steps.title: Paste
steps.body: Mash the olive oil, garlic, rosemary, salt, pepper, Dijon, and lemon juice into a paste. Rub it all over the leg, working it into the scores. Rest at room temp 45 minutes while the pit heats.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: 250°F until the thickest part reads 130-135°F, about 3 to 4 hours depending on size.

steps.title: Rest
steps.body: Rest 20 to 30 minutes tented in foil — the temp will climb a few degrees.

steps.title: Slice and finish
steps.body: Slice against the grain and serve, with the pesto spooned over the top. Save the bone — it makes a hell of a pot of beans.

proTips.text: Lamb wants medium-rare. Past 145°F it tightens up and dries out fast.
Bone-in cooks more evenly and stays juicier than boneless.
Cherry wood gives the crust a beautiful color; oak keeps the smoke in the background.

milestones.label: Served
milestones.hint: Rested, sliced, pesto over the top.

title: Smoked Lamb Chops with Mint Chimichurri
summary: The fast luxury cut. Frenched rib chops kissed with smoke, seared hot, finished with a bright mint chimichurri.
story: Fancy enough for company, easy enough for a weeknight. The smoke stays light, the sear makes the crust, and the chimichurri cuts right through the richness.

items: 8 frenched lamb rib chops, about 1 1/2 inches thick

steps.title: Season
steps.body: Season the chops with olive oil, salt, pepper, granulated garlic, and rosemary. Rest at room temp 30 minutes while the pit heats.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: 225°F until the chops read 120°F inside, about 30 to 40 minutes.

steps.title: Sear
steps.body: Screaming hot — 60 to 90 seconds per side — until the crust darkens and the center reads 130-135°F.

steps.title: Chimichurri
steps.body: While the chops smoke, blitz the chimichurri ingredients until just combined — you want texture, not baby food.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Rest the chops 5 to 10 minutes, then spoon the chimichurri over and serve.

proTips.text: Chops cook fast — the thermometer matters more here than anywhere. They go from perfect to overdone in minutes.
Frenched bones make a great handle. Let people eat with their hands.
Make extra chimichurri. It goes on everything for the next three days.

title: Smoked Stuffed Thanksgiving Turkey
summary: The centerpiece. Dry-brined overnight, stuffed and smoked low, finished hot for crisp skin — with dressing in a pan alongside catching the drippings and the smoke.
story: This is the turkey people talk about all year. The bird gets the cavity stuffing, the rest of the dressing goes in a pan on the smoker — best of both worlds — and a hot finish crisps the skin.

items: 1 lb cornbread, crumbled and dried overnight
1 lb white bread cubes, dried overnight
2 Tbsp fresh sage, chopped (or 2 tsp dried)
3 to 4 cups warm turkey or chicken broth

steps.title: Dry brine
steps.body: Mix the salt, brown sugar, pepper, poultry seasoning, and granulated garlic. Rub all over the bird, inside and out. Refrigerate uncovered 12 to 24 hours.

steps.title: Prep
steps.body: Rinse off the brine and pat dry. Rub the softened butter under the breast skin and the olive oil all over the outside.

steps.title: Inject
steps.body: Stir the Creole seasoning and chicken broth into the melted butter. Inject the breast in a grid pattern, about every 2 inches — the breast is the part that dries out first.

steps.title: Stuff loosely
steps.body: Fill the cavity about two-thirds full with dressing — packed stuffing won't cook through. Truss the legs.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: 275-300°F with apple or cherry until the breast reads 150°F, about 3 1/2 to 4 1/2 hours.

steps.title: Crisp the skin
steps.body: Run the pit up to 375-400°F (or move the bird to a 400°F oven) for the last 30 to 45 minutes, until the skin tightens and browns and the breast hits 165°F — and the stuffing in the cavity reads 165°F.

steps.title: Pan dressing
steps.body: Put the rest of the dressing in a buttered foil pan and smoke it alongside the bird for the last 90 minutes, stirring once.

steps.title: Rest
steps.body: Rest 30 to 45 minutes tented in foil before carving.

proTips.text: The stuffing inside the bird MUST hit 165°F — that's the food-safety line. Thermometer in the center of the cavity stuffing.
The Creole butter injection is non-negotiable on the breast. It's the leanest part of the bird and the first thing to dry out.
The hot finish is what saves the skin. Low smoke alone leaves it rubbery — that last blast at 375-400°F tightens and browns it.
Don't overstuff. A loosely filled cavity cooks through; a packed one stays raw in the middle while the breast dries out.
Save the carcass. Smoked turkey stock is liquid gold for gumbo.

title: Fresh Cranberry-Orange Relish
summary: The bright counterpoint to a rich smoked turkey. Raw cranberries and a whole orange pulsed with sugar — tart, sweet, and bitter in all the right places.
story: Make it the day before; it gets better overnight. The orange peel is the secret — don't peel it.

items: 1 bag (12 oz) fresh cranberries, rinsed and picked over
1 whole navel orange, quartered (peel and all — seeds removed)

steps.title: Pulse
steps.body: Pulse the cranberries and orange quarters in a food processor until finely chopped — not pureed. You want texture.

steps.title: Sweeten
steps.body: Stir in the sugar and the pinch of salt. Start with 3/4 cup; taste and add more if you like it sweeter.

steps.title: Fold
steps.body: Fold in the pecans if using.

steps.title: Rest
steps.body: Refrigerate overnight. The flavors marry and the sugar pulls the juices out.

proTips.text: The orange peel is the secret — don't peel it. That's where the bitter-orange perfume lives.
This freezes beautifully. Make a double batch and freeze half for Christmas.
Leftover relish on a turkey sandwich with mayo is a top-five sandwich experience.

title: Smoked Oyster Casserole
summary: The sleeper hit of the holiday table. Smoky oysters layered with buttery crackers and cream, finished on the smoker until bubbly and golden.
story: The people who wrinkle their nose at oysters always come back for seconds.

items: 2 cans (8 oz each) smoked oysters, drained (or 1 pint fresh oysters, smoked 30 minutes first)
2 sleeves butter crackers (like Ritz), crushed coarse

steps.title: Butter the dish
steps.body: Butter a cast iron skillet or baking dish.

steps.title: Layer
steps.body: Layer half the crushed crackers on the bottom. Scatter the oysters over, drizzle with half the melted butter.

steps.title: Pour
steps.body: Pour the cream and Worcestershire evenly over the top. A few shakes of hot sauce.

steps.title: Top
steps.body: Top with the remaining crackers and the rest of the melted butter.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: 300°F until bubbly and golden on top, 30 to 40 minutes.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Rest 10 minutes, serve with lemon wedges.

proTips.text: Don't oversmoke it — the oysters are already smoked. You're just warming everything through and marrying the flavors.
Butter crackers beat saltines here. The richness is the whole point.
This reheats great. Make it in the morning, warm it back up when the turkey rests.

milestones.label: Layered
milestones.hint: Crackers, oysters, cream in the skillet.

title: Smoked Chicken Wings
wood: Cherry for color, hickory for punch
summary: The cook every pit needs. Smoke first for flavor, finish hot for skin that actually snaps — then toss in whatever sauce the crowd wants.
story: Pat them dry, hit them with baking powder and rub, and don't you dare sauce them before the crisp.

items: 4 lbs chicken wings, split into flats and drumettes, tips removed
2 Tbsp Ember House Rub (or SPG, or lemon-pepper poultry rub)
Your favorite wing sauce, warmed (Buffalo, BBQ, garlic-parmesan — your call)
Ranch or blue cheese, for serving

steps.title: Dry
steps.body: Pat the wings very dry with paper towels — moisture is the enemy of crisp skin.

steps.title: Season and rest
steps.body: Toss with the baking powder and rub until evenly coated. Rest uncovered in the fridge 2 to 4 hours (overnight is even better).

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: 275°F until the wings read 165°F, about 1 1/2 to 2 hours.

steps.title: Crisp
steps.body: Crank the pit to 400°F+ for 10 to 15 minutes, until the skin tightens and crackles.

steps.title: Sauce
steps.body: Toss in warm sauce — or serve dry with sauce on the side. Ranch and celery alongside.

proTips.text: The baking powder is the cheat code. It raises the skin's pH so it browns and crisps instead of going rubbery.
Never sauce before the crisp. Sauce after, always — wet skin never crisps.
These reheat in an air fryer better than fresh out of most ovens. Make extra.

title: Smoked Queso
summary: The dip that disappears first at every cookout. Velveeta, pepper jack, smoked Gouda, sausage, and Rotel, smoked in a foil pan until it's one bubbling golden pot.
story: Scoop with tortilla chips. Stir it while it smokes and don't skip the Velveeta.

items: 1 lb ground breakfast sausage, browned and drained
2 cans (10 oz each) Rotel tomatoes with green chiles, undrained
1 can (4 oz) diced jalapeños, drained (optional, for heat)

steps.title: Brown the sausage
steps.body: Brown the sausage in a skillet, breaking it up fine. Drain well.

steps.title: Load the pan
steps.body: Dump everything into a large disposable foil pan: Velveeta, pepper jack, smoked Gouda, sausage, Rotel, jalapeños if using, and the milk.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: 250°F, stirring every 20 to 30 minutes, until fully melted and bubbly — about 90 minutes.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Serve straight out of the pan with tortilla chips.

proTips.text: Don't skip the stirring. The edges melt first and the middle needs help catching up.
Velveeta is non-negotiable here. Real cheese alone breaks and goes greasy — the Velveeta keeps it smooth.
Add more jalapeño if you want it, or swap in habanero if you're feeling brave. Whichever you choose, dice it fine and stir it in with the rest.
Leftovers (if you're lucky) reheat with a splash of milk, stirred over low heat.

title: Smoked Bologna
summary: Oklahoma prime rib. A whole bologna chub scored in diamonds, rubbed down, and smoked until the outside goes dark and crusty and the inside stays juicy. Slice it thick for sandwiches — this is the one that makes people laugh until they taste it.
story: Serve on white bread with yellow mustard. Don't knock it till you've had it off the pit.

items: 1 whole all-beef bologna chub, 4–5 lbs (not sliced)
1/4 cup yellow mustard, as a binder
1/4 cup Ember House Rub (or your favorite pork rub)
White bread and yellow mustard, for serving

steps.title: Score the chub
steps.body: Peel the casing off the bologna chub if it has one. Score the outside in a diamond pattern, about 1/4 inch deep — this is where the bark builds and the smoke gets in.

steps.title: Bind and rub
steps.body: Slather the whole chub with yellow mustard, then coat it heavy with the rub. Get it in the scores.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 250°F until the outside is dark mahogany with a solid bark — about 3 to 4 hours. It won't take much more color after hour three, so don't chase it.

steps.title: Rest and slice
steps.body: Rest 15 minutes, then slice 1/2-inch thick. Serve on white bread with mustard.

proTips.text: All-beef is the move. The cheap mixed-meat chubs shrink up and split on the pit.
The bark is the whole point — wrapping steams it soft.
Yes, it's bologna. No, nobody's laughing after the first bite.
Leftover slices are gold in a hot skillet the next morning, crisped up for breakfast sandwiches.

milestones.label: Scored and rubbed
milestones.hint: Diamonds cut, mustard and rub on.

title: Smoked Trout
summary: Delicate, smoky, and dead simple. A quick brine, a light smoke, and you've got trout that flakes apart and eats just as good cold the next day on crackers. The hardest part is not eating it all standing at the pit.
story: Serve warm with lemon, or chill it and eat it cold on crackers.

items: 4 whole trout, cleaned (about 12 oz each), or 8 fillets

steps.title: Brine
steps.body: Stir the water, salt, brown sugar, and pepper until dissolved. Submerge the trout and brine in the fridge for 2 hours — no longer, or it goes too salty.

steps.title: Dry and form the pellicle
steps.body: Rinse the fish quick under cold water and pat dry. Lay on a rack in the fridge uncovered for 1 hour so the surface gets tacky. That's the pellicle — smoke sticks to it.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 200°F until the thickest part hits 145°F — about 2 to 3 hours depending on size. The flesh should flake easy.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Serve warm with lemon, or chill it and eat cold on crackers.

proTips.text: The pellicle step matters. Wet fish takes smoke unevenly and the skin goes rubbery — tacky skin takes smoke like a champ.
Don't oversmoke it. Trout is delicate; heavy smoke bulldozes the flavor. Light wood, light hand.
The 2-hour brine is a ceiling, not a floor. Small fillets can go 90 minutes.
Leftover smoked trout mashed with cream cheese, lemon, and dill makes a spread that'll ruin store-bought dip for you.

title: Brown Butter Chocolate Chip Cookies with Pecans
finish: Deep golden crisp edges, chewy centers
summary: Nutty brown butter, melty chocolate, toasted pecans, and a hit of flaky salt — with crisp edges and a chewy middle. These are the cookies that make people ask for the recipe before they finish chewing.
story: The extra yolk and the pan rest are what get you the chew. Pull them when the centers look just barely soft.

items: 2 large eggs plus 1 yolk, room temperature
1 1/2 cups semisweet chocolate chips or chunks
1 cup pecans, toasted and roughly chopped

steps.title: Brown the butter
steps.body: Melt the butter in a light-colored saucepan over medium heat, swirling, until it foams, then turns amber with brown specks and smells nutty — about 5–7 minutes. Pour into a bowl and cool 15 minutes.

steps.title: Mix the dough
steps.body: Whisk the brown butter with both sugars until smooth. Beat in the eggs, yolk, and vanilla. Stir in the flour, baking soda, and kosher salt just until no dry streaks remain. Fold in the chocolate and pecans.

steps.title: Rest
steps.body: Rest the dough 30 minutes at room temp — the flour hydrates and the flavor deepens.

steps.title: Scoop and bake
steps.body: Scoop 2-tablespoon balls onto parchment-lined sheets, 2 inches apart, and press each one down slightly with your palm — flatter cookies crisp at the edges. Sprinkle with flaky salt. Bake at 350°F for 12–14 minutes, until the edges are deep golden and crisp but the centers still look just barely soft.

steps.title: Cool
steps.body: Cool on the pan 10 minutes (they crisp up as they cool), then move to a rack.

proTips.text: Don't walk away from the butter. It goes from brown to burnt fast — pull it when it smells like hazelnuts.
The 30-minute rest is the difference between a good cookie and the one people talk about.
Toast the pecans in a dry skillet 3–4 minutes until fragrant. Raw pecans taste like nothing next to brown butter.
Crisp-chewy is a cooling trick as much as a baking one: pull them when the centers look just barely soft, and the 10-minute pan rest sets the crisp edge while the middle stays chewy.

title: Banana Split Cake
summary: The icebox classic: buttery graham crust, a tangy cream-cheese filling, bananas, pineapple, Cool Whip, and cherries on top. No oven, no fuss — just chill and slice.
story: The cream cheese layer is the whole thing — don't skimp it and don't swap it for pudding mix.

items: 2 packages (8 oz each) cream cheese, softened
1 can (20 oz) crushed pineapple, drained well

steps.title: Make the crust
steps.body: Mix the crumbs, melted butter, and sugar; press firmly into a 9x13 pan. Chill 15 minutes.

steps.title: Make the filling
steps.body: Beat the cream cheese, softened butter, powdered sugar, and vanilla until completely smooth. Spread over the chilled crust.

steps.title: Layer the fruit
steps.body: Layer the banana slices over the filling, then spread the drained pineapple over the bananas.

steps.title: Top and chill
steps.body: Spread the Cool Whip over the top, edge to edge. Chill at least 4 hours — overnight is better.

steps.title: Finish
steps.body: Top with cherries, nuts if using, and a drizzle of chocolate syrup. Slice and serve cold.

proTips.text: Drain that pineapple like you mean it — squeeze it in a clean towel. Wet pineapple makes a soggy cake.
Toss the banana slices in a little lemon juice if you're making it ahead; keeps them from browning.
The cream cheese layer is the whole thing. Don't skimp it and don't swap it for pudding mix.
Chill it overnight. It slices clean and the flavors settle together.

title: Peach Baked Beans
summary: Sweet peaches meet smoky bacon and brown sugar in beans that go from side dish to the thing people ask about. Built for the smoker, but the oven works fine.
story: Bush's Brown Sugar beans and peach pie filling do the heavy lifting — the pit does the rest.

items: 2 cans (28 oz each) Bush's Brown Sugar baked beans
1 can (21 oz) peach pie filling, roughly chopped
Salt and black pepper to taste

steps.title: Crisp the bacon
steps.body: Cook the chopped bacon until crisp. Pull it out and leave the drippings in the pan.

steps.title: Soften the onion
steps.body: Sauté the onion (and bell pepper, if using) in the drippings until soft, about 5 minutes.

steps.title: Mix
steps.body: Stir everything into a 9x13 pan or cast-iron skillet: beans, pie filling, brown sugar, BBQ sauce, mustard, molasses, paprika, bacon, and onion. Season with salt and pepper.

steps.title: Bake or smoke
steps.body: Bake at 350°F for about 1 hour, until thick and bubbly with a caramelized top — or smoke at 275°F for 2 hours for extra pit flavor.

steps.title: Rest
steps.body: Rest 10 minutes. They thicken as they cool.

proTips.text: The Bush's beans and pie filling already bring sweetness, so the added brown sugar is cut back — taste before you add more.
Chop the pie filling a little; the peach slices are big and spread better cut down.
These are better the next day. Make them ahead and reheat.
If they get too thick, splash in a little water or peach juice.

title: Key Lime Coleslaw
summary: Bright, tangy, and cool — key lime juice and zest cut through rich smoked meat like nothing else. Built for pulled pork sandwiches and fish tacos.
story: Bottled key lime juice is fine — nobody's squeezing 30 key limes on a weeknight.

items: 1 bag (14 oz) coleslaw mix (or 1 small head cabbage, shredded, plus 1 grated carrot)
1/4 cup key lime juice (about 6–8 key limes)

steps.title: Make the dressing
steps.body: Whisk the mayo, sour cream, key lime juice, zest, sugar, salt, and pepper until smooth.

steps.title: Toss
steps.body: Toss with the slaw mix, grated bell pepper, green onions, and cilantro until everything's coated.

steps.title: Chill
steps.body: Chill at least 1 hour — it gets better as it sits.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Toss again before serving. Taste and add more lime or salt.

proTips.text: Bottled key lime juice is fine — nobody's squeezing 30 key limes on a weeknight.
Don't dress it more than 4 hours ahead or it goes watery. An hour is the sweet spot.
This is the slaw for pulled pork sandwiches and blackened fish tacos.

title: Smoked Shrimp Po'Boy
summary: Plump Gulf shrimp kissed with smoke, piled into crisp French bread with spicy remoulade, shredded lettuce, tomato, and pickles. Mississippi Gulf Coast in a sandwich.
story: Gulf shrimp if you can get them — Mississippi shrimpers know what they're doing.

items: 1 1/2 lbs large shrimp, peeled and deveined
2 tbsp olive oil or melted butter

steps.title: Season the shrimp
steps.body: Toss the shrimp with the oil, Cajun seasoning, garlic powder, and paprika. Rest 15 minutes.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 225°F for 30–45 minutes, until pink and firm (145°F internal). Don't overcook — shrimp go fast.

steps.title: Make the remoulade
steps.body: Stir the remoulade ingredients together. Chill until serving.

steps.title: Toast the bread
steps.body: Butter the rolls and toast cut-side down in a skillet or on the smoker until golden.

steps.title: Build it
steps.body: Remoulade on both sides, lettuce, tomato, pickles, then a heap of smoked shrimp. More remoulade on top.

proTips.text: Gulf shrimp if you can get them — Mississippi shrimpers know what they're doing.
Shrimp overcook in a blink. Pull them the second they're pink and curled into a C.
Dress it right before serving so the bread stays crisp.
Toasting the bread in butter is not optional.

title: Smoked Whole Duck
finish: 160°F in the breast, 170°F in the thigh
summary: A whole duck, injected and smoked low over fruit wood until the skin turns crisp and golden — with a drip pan of liquid gold underneath.
story: Kelly injects most of his fowl — turkey, duck, all of it. The injection keeps the lean breast juicy while the smoker does its work, and scoring the skin lets the fat render out instead of going rubbery. Finish hot for the crackle. Save every drop of fat from the drip pan; that is liquid gold for potatoes.

steps.title: Inject the bird
steps.body: Whisk the injection ingredients until smooth. Inject all through the breast, thighs, and legs — a little in each spot; do not overfill one place.

steps.title: Score and season
steps.body: Pat the duck completely dry, inside and out. Score the skin in a crosshatch pattern, cutting through the fat but not into the meat. Season all over and inside the cavity. Tuck the orange quarters inside if using.

steps.title: Rest
steps.body: Rest uncovered in the fridge overnight if you can — that is the crispy-skin secret. At least 1 hour if not.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 250°F, breast-side up, with a drip pan underneath to catch the fat. Apple or cherry wood. Smoke 3–4 hours until the breast reads 160°F and the thigh reads 170°F.

steps.title: Crisp the skin
steps.body: Crank the pit to 400°F for the last 15–20 minutes for crackling skin.

steps.title: Rest and carve
steps.body: Rest 15–20 minutes before carving so the juices settle.

proTips: Save every drop of fat from the drip pan — duck fat is liquid gold for potatoes.
Do not skip the scoring. That is how the fat renders out instead of staying rubbery.
Fruit wood is the classic pairing for duck.

title: Pepper Jelly Glazed Smoked Oxtails
finish: Meat pulls easily from the bone
summary: Smoke, braise till they surrender, then lacquer in a sweet-heat pepper jelly glaze. Sticky, beefy, and not like anybody else's oxtails.
story: Kelly had never cooked oxtails before this one. Most recipes go Jamaican-style or straight BBQ sauce — this one goes sweet-heat instead. Pepper jelly, a Southern grocery staple, reduces with the braising liquid into a sticky glaze that clings to every piece. Smoke first for the bark, braise till the meat gives up, glaze till it shines.

steps.title: Season
steps.body: Season the oxtails all over. Rest 1 hour, or overnight in the fridge.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 250°F over hickory or oak, 3 hours, until the bark sets.

steps.title: Braise
steps.body: Move to a Dutch oven or foil pan with the onion, garlic, and beef broth. Cover tight. Braise at 275°F (smoker or oven) 2½–3 hours, until the meat pulls from the bone.

steps.title: Make the glaze
steps.body: Lift out the oxtails. Strain the braising liquid and skim the fat. Simmer 1 cup of the liquid with the pepper jelly, vinegar, and Worcestershire until thick and sticky.

steps.title: Glaze and serve
steps.body: Toss the oxtails in the glaze until every piece shines. Serve over rice or grits.

proTips: Red pepper jelly gives color; green gives a fresher bite. Both work.
The vinegar keeps the sweetness from going candy — do not skip it.
Make extra glaze. People will ask for it.
These reheat beautifully. Arguably better the next day.

title: Pork Belly Burnt Ends
summary: Meat candy. Barky pork belly cubes braised in butter, brown sugar, and honey, then lacquered in Kelly's Ember Finishing Glaze.
story: Burnt ends started as the barky trimmings Kansas City pitmasters gave away — now they are the bite everybody fights over. Cubed belly takes the same treatment: smoke for bark, braise till the fat renders, then glaze. Kelly finishes his in his own Ember Finishing Glaze, and that sweet-heat lacquer is what makes the pile shine.

items: 1 whole pork belly (8–10 lb), skin removed
1 cup Kelly's Ember Finishing Glaze (or your favorite BBQ sauce)

steps.title: Cube and rub
steps.body: Cut the belly into 1½-inch cubes, keeping them even so they cook alike. Toss in the rub until coated on all sides.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 250°F over hickory, 3 hours, until the bark sets and the edges crisp.

steps.title: Braise
steps.body: Move to a foil pan. Scatter the butter over, then the brown sugar and honey. Cover tight with foil. Back on the smoker 1½–2 hours, until probe-tender — the probe slides in like butter.

steps.title: Glaze
steps.body: Drain off most of the liquid. Toss the cubes in Kelly's Ember Finishing Glaze until every piece shines.

steps.title: Tack up
steps.body: Back on the smoker uncovered 15–20 minutes to set the glaze.

proTips: Even cubes matter more than anything. Small ones dry out, big ones stay chewy.
Do not skip the covered braise — that is what renders the fat down.
Go light on the final sauce. They should shine, not swim.

title: Honey Garlic Glaze
finish: Thick enough to coat a spoon
summary: Sweet, savory, sticky — with an Asian lean. Honey, garlic, hoisin, and soy. Goes good on pork, chicken, whatever your taste desires.
story: Kelly wanted a glaze with an Asian lean for pork loin or belly, and asked for hoisin in it. The hoisin brings the deep savory-sweet backbone, the honey brings the shine, and the garlic and ginger do the talking. Brush it on in the last stretch of the cook — it burns fast over direct heat.

items: 1/2 tsp red pepper flakes (optional, for heat)

steps.title: Combine
steps.body: Combine the honey, hoisin, soy sauce, garlic, vinegar, ginger, and pepper flakes in a small saucepan.

steps.title: Simmer
steps.body: Bring to a gentle simmer over medium heat, stirring, 4–5 minutes until the garlic softens and it thickens slightly.

steps.title: Finish
steps.body: Take off the heat and stir in the sesame oil.

steps.title: Use it
steps.body: Brush over pork, chicken, or whatever your taste desires in the last 15–20 minutes of the cook, or toss cubes in it to finish.

proTips: The sesame oil goes in off the heat — it turns bitter if it boils.
This burns fast over direct heat. Last 15–20 minutes only, or use it as a finishing toss.
The hoisin makes it thick enough on its own — no cornstarch needed.
Double it. It disappears.

title: Deer Camp Smoked Venison Stew
summary: A stick-to-your-ribs stew. Seared venison braised low in a Dutch oven on the smoker with root vegetables and tomatoes, so the whole pot picks up that wood flavor.
story: Kelly asked for a venison stew with tomatoes in it — diced from a can, or whole ones quartered up when you've got them. The Dutch oven goes straight on the smoker so the braise drinks in the smoke while the venison goes tender.

items: 2 lbs venison stew meat (shoulder or hindquarter), cut in 1½-inch chunks
1 can (14.5 oz) diced tomatoes, or 3–4 whole tomatoes, quartered

steps.title: Sear
steps.body: Season the venison with salt and pepper. Heat the oil in a Dutch oven over medium-high and sear the meat in batches until browned on all sides. Set aside.

steps.title: Build the base
steps.body: In the same pot, cook the onion until soft, about 5 minutes. Stir in the garlic and tomato paste and cook 1 minute more.

steps.title: Braise
steps.body: Pour in the beef broth and tomatoes, scraping up the browned bits. Stir in the Worcestershire, thyme, and bay leaves. Return the venison to the pot.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Cover and place on the smoker at 275°F for 2 hours.

steps.title: Vegetables
steps.body: Stir in the carrots, potatoes, and celery. Cover and cook 1 to 1½ hours more, until the meat is fork-tender and the vegetables are soft.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Fish out the bay leaves, rest 10 minutes, and serve.

proTips: Venison is lean, so don't rush it — if the meat fights the fork, it needs more time, not more heat.
Sear in batches. Crowding the pot steams the meat instead of browning it.
This is even better the next day, once the flavors settle in.

title: Smoked Venison Shepherd's Pie
summary: Ground venison in a savory gravy with peas, carrots, and corn, under a smoked cheddar mashed potato crust. The whole skillet goes on the smoker until the top turns golden.
story: Kelly said this one was made exactly the way he'd make it — no notes. The fork-ridged mash isn't just for looks: those ridges are what turn brown and crispy in the smoke.

items: 2½ lbs russet potatoes, peeled and chunked

steps.title: Brown
steps.body: Brown the venison in a large cast iron skillet over medium-high heat, breaking it up. Drain off any liquid. Season with salt and pepper.

steps.title: Vegetables
steps.body: Add the onion and carrots; cook 5 minutes until softened. Stir in the garlic and tomato paste; cook 1 minute.

steps.title: Gravy
steps.body: Sprinkle in the flour and stir 1 minute. Pour in the broth, scraping the pan. Stir in the Worcestershire and thyme. Simmer 5 minutes until it thickens into a gravy, then fold in the peas and corn. Spread it level.

steps.title: Mash
steps.body: Boil the potatoes until fork-tender, about 15 minutes. Drain, then mash with the butter, milk, salt, and smoked cheddar until smooth.

steps.title: Top
steps.body: Spread the mash over the meat, edge to edge. Rough up the top with a fork so the ridges catch the smoke and crisp.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Place the skillet on the smoker at 375°F for 25–30 minutes, until the top is golden and the edges are bubbling. Rest 10 minutes before serving.

proTips: Those fork ridges aren't just for looks — they're what turn brown and crispy in the smoke.
Drain the venison well after browning so the gravy stays rich, not watery.
A 12-inch cast iron skillet is the perfect vessel — stovetop to smoker, no extra dishes.

title: Smoke and Ember Venison Pot Roast
summary: The Mississippi-style roast, translated for deer and branded our way. Ranch, au jus, a whole stick of butter, and pepperoncini — plus new potatoes, baby carrots, celery, and tomatoes, all braised in one Dutch oven on the smoker.
story: Kelly wanted this one named Smoke and Ember Venison Pot Roast, and he built it like a full one-pot meal: whole new potatoes, baby carrots, celery, and tomatoes go in around the roast so nothing's missing when the lid comes off. The butter does the work the fat would do on a beef chuck, since venison runs lean.

items: 3–4 lb venison roast (hindquarter, neck, or shoulder)
6–8 pepperoncini peppers, plus a splash of the juice
1 can (14.5 oz) diced tomatoes, or 3–4 whole tomatoes, quartered

steps.title: Sear
steps.body: Season the roast generously with salt and pepper. Sear it hard on all sides in a Dutch oven over medium-high heat.

steps.title: Season
steps.body: Sprinkle the ranch seasoning and au jus mix evenly over the roast. Lay the stick of butter right on top. Scatter the pepperoncini around it and add a splash of their juice.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Cover and place on the smoker at 275°F for 2 hours.

steps.title: Vegetables
steps.body: Nestle the potatoes, carrots, celery, and tomatoes around the roast. Cover and cook 1½–2 hours more, until the meat shreds easily and the vegetables are tender.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Shred the meat right in the pot, stir everything through the juices, and serve.

proTips: Don't lift the lid to peek — venison dries out fast when the pot loses its steam.
If it fights the fork, give it another 30 minutes, not more heat.
The vegetables go in late on purpose — 4 hours would turn them to mush.

title: Harold's Smoked Venison Summer Sausage
summary: Classic deer-camp sausage. Venison mixed with pork or beef fat for the richness it lacks, seasoned with mustard seed and garlic, then slow-smoked in fibrous casings.
story: Named for Harold Caldwell, one of the three men the venison page is dedicated to. Kelly ran this one by his buddy, who said that's exactly how he does his. The fat can be pork or beef — cook's choice. The curing salt and the overnight rest are non-negotiable: low-temp smoking without cure isn't safe, and the rest is where the tang develops.

items: 2 lbs ground pork or beef fat (the fat the venison's missing)
Fibrous sausage casings, about 2½ inch diameter

steps.title: Mix
steps.body: Mix the venison, pork or beef fat, all the seasonings, and the cold water in a big bowl until it gets sticky and tacky — about 2 minutes of real mixing. That's what binds it.

steps.title: Stuff and rest
steps.body: Stuff into the casings firmly, squeezing out air pockets, and tie the ends. Refrigerate overnight, 12–24 hours, so the cure does its work and the flavors marry.

steps.title: Dry
steps.body: Hang or lay on the smoker at 130°F for 1 hour with no smoke, just to dry the casings.

steps.title: Smoke low
steps.body: Raise to 150°F with smoke for 2 hours.

steps.title: Finish
steps.body: Raise to 175°F and smoke until the internal temp hits 152°F, about 3–4 hours more.

steps.title: Chill
steps.body: Straight into an ice bath for 15 minutes to stop the cooking. Hang at room temp 1 hour to bloom, then refrigerate.

proTips: Don't skip the curing salt and don't skip the overnight rest — low-temp smoking without cure isn't safe.
Mix until tacky. Under-mixed sausage crumbles when you slice it.
The ice bath isn't optional — it stops the cook and keeps the texture snappy.
Make it your own: fold in a cup of diced pepper jack cheese, diced jalapeños, or both — whatever sounds good — right along with the seasonings.

title: Deer Camp Sweet Heat Chili
summary: Not your standard chili. Bush's baked beans bring the sweet, chipotles and hatch chiles bring the smoky heat, and the whole pot rides the smoker over pecan or maple wood.
story: Kelly wanted this one different from the regular chili recipes out there — sweet and spicy, with Bush's baked beans and kidney beans. The hatch chiles were his call, and so was the light wood: pecan or maple, so the smoke stays sweet with the beans.

items: 2 hatch chiles, roasted, peeled, and diced (or 1 can diced hatch chiles)
2 chipotle peppers in adobo, minced, plus 1 Tbsp adobo sauce
1 can (28 oz) Bush's baked beans, undrained
Shredded cheddar, sour cream, and sliced green onions, for serving

steps.title: Brown
steps.body: Brown the venison in a Dutch oven over medium-high heat, breaking it up. Drain off any liquid and season with salt and pepper.

steps.title: Vegetables and spices
steps.body: Add the onion, bell pepper, and hatch chiles; cook 5 minutes until soft. Stir in the garlic, chili powder, smoked paprika, cumin, and oregano; cook 1 minute until fragrant.

steps.title: Beans
steps.body: Stir in the chipotles and adobo sauce, then the baked beans (with their sauce — that's the sweetness), kidney beans, tomatoes, and broth.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Cover and place on the smoker over pecan or maple wood at 275°F for 2–3 hours, stirring once or twice, until thick and rich. (Stovetop works too: simmer 1 hour, partially covered.)

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Serve with cheddar, sour cream, and green onions.

proTips: Don't drain the baked beans — their sauce is what makes this chili sweet.
The chipotle heat builds as it sits, so go easy if you're serving it straight off the smoker.
Pecan or maple keeps the smoke sweet with the beans — hickory would bully the sweetness.

title: Abby's Lemon Pepper Trout
summary: Simple and clean. The trout goes on the grill skin-down, butter melts over the top, lemon pepper does the rest.
story: Named for Kelly's daughter Abby. Kelly's take on trout: lemon pepper and butter, straight on the grill over a light wood.

items: 4 whole trout (about 10–12 oz each), cleaned, or 8 fillets
Fresh dill or parsley, chopped, for serving

steps.title: Season
steps.body: Pat the trout dry. Rub the outside (or both sides of fillets) with olive oil and season generously with lemon pepper, inside and out.

steps.title: Butter and lemon
steps.body: Stuff a couple lemon slices and a spoonful of butter inside each fish (or lay lemon slices and butter pats over fillets).

steps.title: Grill
steps.body: Grill over indirect heat at 275°F with a light wood — alder or apple — for 25–35 minutes, until the flesh flakes easily and hits 145°F.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Shower with fresh dill and serve with the remaining lemon.

proTips: Don't flip it. Skin-down the whole cook keeps the delicate flesh intact and lets the butter baste down through.
Alder or apple keeps the smoke light — heavy woods overpower trout.

title: Megan and David's Smoked Catfish
summary: Southern staple, done right. A simple brine, a Cajun crust, and a mild wood smoke — fillets go on skin-down and never flip.
story: Named for Megan and David. Kelly's rules for catfish: brine it, trim the red meat off wild-caught fillets, and keep the wood mild — pecan, alder, or maple, never hickory.

items: 3 Tbsp Cajun seasoning (store-bought works, or mix: 1 Tbsp paprika, 2 tsp garlic powder, 2 tsp onion powder, 2 tsp salt, 1 tsp black pepper, 1 tsp cayenne, 1 tsp dried thyme)

steps.title: Brine
steps.body: Dissolve the salt and brown sugar in the cold water, add the bay leaves, peppercorns, and lemon, and submerge the fillets for 1–2 hours in the fridge. Rinse and pat dry. Don't go longer than 2 hours — fish gets mushy past that.

steps.title: Trim and season
steps.body: If working with wild-caught catfish, trim the dark red meat off the fillets — that's where the muddy taste lives. Brush with olive oil and coat generously with Cajun seasoning on both sides.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 225°F over a mild wood — pecan, alder, or maple — skin-down, for 1½–2 hours, until the fish flakes easily and hits 145°F.

steps.title: Butter and serve
steps.body: Brush with melted butter in the last 15 minutes. Serve with lemon wedges.

proTips: Catfish skin sticks — oil the grates well or lay the fillets on foil with holes poked in it.
Don't flip. The skin side protects the flesh from the heat.
Keep the wood mild — hickory would bully the fish.

title: Oliver's Oreos
summary: Bacon-wrapped smoked Oreos from Bub & Sissy's Sweet Shop. Sweet, salty, smoky — the cookie goes soft and cake-like inside crisp bacon.
story: Named for Oliver, Kelly's grandson, and the featured treat at Bub & Sissy's Sweet Shop.

items: 1 pack Oreo cookies (regular, not Double Stuf)

steps.title: Wrap
steps.body: Wrap each Oreo in one slice of bacon, overlapping the seam underneath. Pin with a toothpick.

steps.title: Sweeten
steps.body: Dust each one lightly with brown sugar.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 275°F over apple or cherry wood for 60–90 minutes, until the bacon is crisp and browned.

steps.title: Rest
steps.body: Rest 10 minutes — the filling comes out molten. Pull the toothpicks before serving.

title: Brooklyn's Brownies
finish: Edges set, center just barely jiggles
summary: Smoked skillet brownies from Bub & Sissy's Sweet Shop. Fudgy dark chocolate loaded with walnuts and pecans, kissed with cherry wood smoke.
story: Named for Brooklyn, Kelly's granddaughter — Sissy herself — and baked for the sweet shop.

items: 8 oz semi-sweet chocolate chips (about 1 1/3 cups), plus 1/2 cup more for the top
Flaky sea salt, for the top (optional)

steps.title: Melt
steps.body: Melt the butter and 8 oz chocolate together; cool 5 minutes.

steps.title: Mix
steps.body: Whisk in both sugars, then the eggs one at a time, then the vanilla.

steps.title: Fold
steps.body: Fold in the flour, cocoa, and salt just until combined. Fold in the extra 1/2 cup chips, the walnuts, and the pecans.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Pour into a buttered 10-inch cast iron skillet. Smoke at 325°F over cherry or apple wood for 35–45 minutes, until the edges are set and the center just barely jiggles.

steps.title: Rest
steps.body: Rest 20 minutes — the center firms up as it cools. Sprinkle flaky salt, cut, and serve.

title: Smoked Deviled Eggs
summary: Real smoked deviled eggs — the eggs go on the smoker raw in the shell and come off hard-boiled with smoke all the way through.
story: No shortcuts here: the eggs cook right on the smoker in their shells, so the smoke gets into the egg itself, not just the filling. Kelly likes his deviled eggs just a touch sweet — enough to taste it, never enough to argue with the smoke.
school: Smoke the eggs in the shell — the shell takes the smoke and the egg takes the flavor. An ice bath right off the smoker is what makes them peel clean.

items: Crumbled crispy bacon or thin jalapeño slices, for the top (optional)

steps.title: Fire up
steps.body: Get the smoker to 225°F with apple or cherry wood rolling thin and blue.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Set the eggs right on the grate, in the shell. Smoke 2 hours, turning them once at the hour mark.

steps.title: Ice bath
steps.body: Drop the eggs straight into an ice bath for 15 minutes — that's what makes them peel clean.

steps.title: Fill
steps.body: Peel, halve lengthwise, and pop the yolks into a bowl. Mash with the mayo, mustard, relish, sugar, vinegar, salt, and pepper until smooth.

steps.title: Finish
steps.body: Spoon or pipe the filling back into the whites. Dust with smoked paprika and top with bacon or jalapeño if you're feeling it.

steps.title: Chill
steps.body: Chill at least 30 minutes before serving — they're better cold.

title: Fair-Style Smoked Turkey Legs
finish: 175°F internal, meat pulling back from the bone
summary: Big, juicy, smoky turkey legs just like the state fair — brined overnight, rubbed down, and smoked till tender.
story: Everybody remembers their first fair turkey leg — the size of it, the smoky smell, eating it walking around with juice running down your arm. These are that leg. An overnight salt-and-brown-sugar brine keeps them juicy, a paprika rub builds the crust, and 275°F of hickory or pecan smoke does the rest. Take them to 175°F so the meat pulls back from the bone and eats tender, not tough.

items: 1 tsp cayenne, optional for a little kick

steps.title: Brine overnight
steps.body: Stir the water, salt, and brown sugar until dissolved. Submerge the legs and brine in the fridge 8 to 12 hours, or overnight.

steps.title: Rinse and rub
steps.body: Pull the legs out, rinse, and pat dry. Let them sit out 30 minutes to take the chill off. Mix the rub ingredients and coat the legs all over.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 275°F for 3 to 4 hours, until the meat hits 175°F internal and pulls back from the bone a little. If they're getting dark, wrap in foil for the last hour.

steps.title: Rest
steps.body: Rest 15 minutes before serving.

proTips: The fair legs have that pink, ham-like look from curing salt. If you can find it, add 1 tsp curing salt to the brine — totally optional, still great without it.
